"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2432: the indentation-tab detector for numbered code listings.

What it does: this component goes strongly negative on the indentation whitespace that
follows a line number in a numbered listing, the text a viewer shows as

      357<TAB>                await user.click(prevButton);

The more indentation follows the number's tab, the more negative it gets. A bare tab with
nothing after it is weaker. Ordinary indentation after a real newline is ignored (about 0),
and so is every token that is not whitespace.

Smaller cases get the same kind of response:
  - indentation at the start of a line that is only a diff marker ("+" or "-"), or only a
    grep-style line number with ":" or "-" ("715:", "526-"), is moderately negative;
  - indentation after a literal backslash-n (code escaped inside a string, e.g.
    "...{\\n    return x;\\n...") is moderately negative;
  - a literal backslash-t token (the two characters "\\t") is mildly negative;
  - a word directly after the number's tab ("\timport") is only weakly negative.

It keeps the text of the current line so far (read back from the newest tokens) and needs
nothing else; the carry is unused.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# The current line so far plus this token's leading whitespace is "<spaces><digits><TAB>"
# followed only by whitespace: the line-number tab of a numbered listing, then indentation.
NUMBERED_TAB = re.compile(r"^[ \t]*\d+\t[ \t]*$")
# A line that is only a diff marker, or only a grep-style line number and ":" or "-".
DIFF_MARK = re.compile(r"^[+\-]$")
GREP_LABEL = re.compile(r"^[ \t]*\d+[:\-]$")
WHITESPACE = " \t\xa0"


def _leading_ws(text):
    return text[: len(text) - len(text.lstrip(WHITESPACE))]


def _line_before(prefix):
    """The text on the current line before the newest token."""
    pieces = []
    for piece in reversed(prefix.token_strings[:-1]):
        if "\n" in piece:
            pieces.append(piece.split("\n")[-1])
            break
        pieces.append(piece)
    return "".join(reversed(pieces))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    lead = _leading_ws(token)
    line = _line_before(prefix)

    # 1. Indentation right after a line number's tab in a numbered listing.
    if lead and NUMBERED_TAB.match(line + lead):
        if lead != token:  # a word follows the indentation, e.g. "\timport"
            return None, -0.5
        if "\t" not in lead:  # spaces only, after a numbered line's tab
            return None, -min(4.5, 0.14 * len(lead))
        if len(lead) == 1:  # a bare tab, nothing indented after it
            return None, -3.0
        return None, -min(7.5, 4.9 + 0.1 * len(lead))

    # 2. Indentation that opens a diff line or a grep-style labelled line.
    if lead and lead == token and (DIFF_MARK.match(line) or GREP_LABEL.match(line)):
        return None, -2.0

    # 3. Indentation after a literal backslash-n (escaped code inside a string).
    if lead and lead == token and line.endswith("\\n"):
        return None, -min(4.2, 2.0 + 0.2 * len(lead))

    # 4. A literal backslash-t token, e.g. escaped tabs in a string.
    if token in ("\\t", "\\t\\t"):
        return None, -1.3

    return None, 0.0

"""Layer-1 MLP down-projection component 2435, as a readable rule.

What the component is: a linear read-out of layer 1's MLP hidden state. Almost everywhere
it is close to zero (typically within 0.1), with no simple lexical rule behind most of its
small values. Two things are clear enough to write down:

1. A "Title:" header at the very start of a document. When a document opens with the word
   Title (or its Chinese equivalent 标题) and the next token is a colon, the component fires
   very strongly (about 10, the largest value it takes). Mid-document "Title:" does not.

2. The first token of a document has no earlier context in the model's attention, so its
   value depends only on the token itself. Sentence-opening capitalised words are mildly
   positive, markdown headings ("#", "##") more so, and other tokens sit near zero.

Everywhere else the program predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()

# Document-opening words that turn a following colon into a large activation.
TITLE_WORDS = {"Title": 10.1, "标题": 9.9}


def doc_start(prefix, i):
    """True if token i is the first token of its document (position 0 or a new document id)."""
    return i == 0 or prefix.document_ids[i] != prefix.document_ids[i - 1]


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[t]
    if word == ":" and t >= 1 and prefix.token_strings[t - 1] in TITLE_WORDS:
        if doc_start(prefix, t - 1):
            return carry, TITLE_WORDS[prefix.token_strings[t - 1]]
    if doc_start(prefix, t):
        if word in ("#", "##"):
            return carry, 0.5
        if word[:1].isupper():
            return carry, 0.15
        return carry, 0.05
    return carry, 0.0

"""Footballer-suffix detector: component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2436.

The component is sparse: most tokens sit near 0, and its large responses come from a few
word-level contexts. Its dominant response is the "er" that completes "footballer":
when the model has just read "football" (or "Football") and the next token is "er"/"ers",
the component reads about +4.3. That is the word "footballer" being spelled out, as in
"rugby league football|er, born ..." or "John Flood (football|er)".

Smaller rules, all stated plainly:
- "Football" followed by "League", "Club", "Federation", "Cup", "team" (and plurals): about +1.
- The first token of each document has no left context. The component gives it about +0.14,
  the average over document starts (it varies by token, roughly -0.4 to +0.7).
- The repeated middle-dot token "··" (a dotted leader fill) gives about -0.98.
- Everything else is 0.

On the eval rows this explains about 9% of the variance (Pearson r about 0.31); the
football-"er" rule carries nearly all of that. The rest of the variance is diffuse: no concept
found in the data (compound-noun heads, sports words, filler) separates its positive from
its negative responses, so a token table would add accuracy but no understanding.
"""

READS = ()

TEAM_WORDS = ("league", "club", "clubs", "federation", "cup", "team", "teams")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.14                      # first token of a document
    if cur == "··":
        return carry, -0.98                     # dotted-leader filler token
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 else ""
    if before == "football":
        if cur.lower() in ("er", "ers"):
            return carry, 4.3                   # "football" + "er" -> footballer
        if cur.lower() in TEAM_WORDS:
            return carry, 1.0                   # "Football League", "Football Club", ...
    return carry, 0.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2437 -- a line-initial declaration detector.

What it does: this component writes a signed signal into the residual stream. It is large
and positive when a line *begins* with a word that opens a declaration in statically typed
code: `public` most of all, then `private`, `int`, `void`, `bool`, `protected`, `static`, and
similar. It is negative when a line begins with a divider or bullet (`---`, `+++`, `-`, `>`,
`!`), or with a word from TypeScript, JavaScript or API-doc style (`type`, `get`, `set`,
`async`, `constructor`, `interface`, `method`, `package`, `export`). Everywhere else in the
text, including mid-line, it is near zero.

The program keeps one bit of state, `line_start`: whether the text since the last newline
is only spaces or tabs. It resets at each document start, where the first token is also
treated as line-initial.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that open a declaration when they start a line, with the typical signed activation.
DECLARATION = {
    "public": 1.5,
    "procedure": 1.2,
    "bool": 0.9,
    "private": 0.8,
    "int": 0.8,
    "void": 0.75,
    "protected": 0.7,
    "double": 0.6,
    "namespace": 0.6,
    "func": 0.55,
    "float": 0.4,
    "static": 0.4,
    "long": 0.3,
    "struct": 0.3,
}

# Words and marks that start a line and push the signal negative.
NEGATIVE = {
    "type": -1.7,
    "get": -1.4,
    "async": -2.0,
    "constructor": -2.0,
    "interface": -1.2,
    "method": -0.9,
    "package": -0.6,
    "export": -0.5,
    "set": -0.4,
    ">": -0.7,
    "!": -0.5,
    "-": -0.3,
    "--": -0.3,
}


def _is_rule(word):
    """A divider such as `---`, `~~` or `+++`: a run of one mark, at least two long."""
    return len(word) >= 2 and word[0] in "-~+" and len(set(word)) == 1 and word not in NEGATIVE


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: True if the text since the last newline is only blanks (always True at a doc start).
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc_start = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    line_start = True if doc_start or carry is None else carry
    word = token.strip(" \t\r\n")
    value = 0.0
    if line_start:
        if word in DECLARATION:
            value = DECLARATION[word]
        elif word in NEGATIVE:
            value = NEGATIVE[word]
        elif _is_rule(word):
            value = -1.2
    # The next token starts a line if this one ends in a newline after only blanks.
    if "\n" in token:
        next_line_start = token.rsplit("\n", 1)[1].strip(" \t") == ""
    else:
        next_line_start = line_start and token.strip(" \t") == ""
    return next_line_start, value

Chinese/Japanese 'two/both' spellings produce the largest values, reduced
when fused into longer tokens. Chinese 两/兩 also raise the following token.
A fixed multilingual cardinal vocabulary is matched against the word so far:
split words respond more than whole words, and whole English cardinals are
weakly negative. There are small rules for 'several', romanized 'liang',
document starts and paired middle dots. This is not general number parsing.
"""

READS = ()
GROUPS = (
    # The first group has dedicated, very common English word tokens.
    'two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve thirteen '
    'fourteen fifteen sixteen seventeen eighteen nineteen twenty thirty '
    'forty fifty sixty seventy eighty ninety hundred thousand',
    # Spanish
    'dos tres cuatro cinco seis siete ocho nueve diez once doce trece '
    'catorce quince veinte treinta cuarenta cincuenta sesenta setenta ochenta noventa',
    # French
    'deux trois quatre cinq six sept huit neuf dix onze douze treize '
    'quatorze quinze seize vingt trente quarante cinquante soixante',
    # Italian
    'due tre quattro cinque sei sette otto nove dieci undici dodici '
    'venti trenta quaranta cinquanta sessanta settanta ottanta novanta',
    # Portuguese
    'dois duas três quatro cinco seis sete oito nove dez onze doze treze '
    'catorze quinze vinte trinta quarenta cinquenta sessenta setenta oitenta noventa',
    # German
    'zwei drei vier fünf sechs sieben acht neun zehn elf zwölf '
    'zwanzig dreißig vierzig fünfzig sechzig siebzig achtzig neunzig',
    # Dutch
    'twee drie vier vijf zes zeven acht negen tien elf twaalf twintig dertig veertig',
    # Swedish
    'två tre fyra fem sex sju åtta nio tio tjugo trettio fyrtio',
    # Turkish
    'iki üç dört beş altı yedi sekiz dokuz on',
    # Polish
    'dwa dwie trzy cztery pięć sześć siedem osiem dziewięć dziesięć',
    # Russian
    'два две три четыре пять шесть семь восемь девять десять',
)

ENGLISH = set(GROUPS[0].split())
FOREIGN = set(' '.join(GROUPS[1:]).split()) - ENGLISH
AMBIGUOUS = {'on', 'sex', 'once', 'elf', 'seize', 'sei', 'otto'}
ITALIAN_CUES = {
    'il', 'gli', 'di', 'che', 'della', 'delle', 'dei', 'nella', 'sono',
}
FRENCH_CUES = {'le', 'les', 'des', 'dans', 'une', 'pour', 'avec', 'est', 'au'}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    first = carry is None or carry[0] != doc
    if first:
        previous, word, recent, after_two = b'', '', '', False
    else:
        previous, word, recent, after_two = carry[1:]
    raw = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    text = raw.decode('utf-8', errors='ignore')
    completed = (previous + raw).decode('utf-8', errors='ignore')
    split_word = bool(word and text and text[0].isalpha())
    pieces = re.split(r'[\W\d_]+', text.lower())
    word = (word + pieces[0])[-40:] if len(pieces) == 1 else pieces[-1]
    recent = (recent + text)[-160:]

    value = (-0.19 if raw.startswith(b' ') else -0.36) if first else 0.0
    if word in ENGLISH:
        value += 0.6 if split_word else -0.07
    elif word in FOREIGN:
        value += 1.0 if split_word else 0.25
        if word in AMBIGUOUS:
            value = 0.0
        elif word in {'due', 'sept'}:
            cues = ITALIAN_CUES if word == 'due' else FRENCH_CUES
            local_words = set(re.findall(r'[^\W\d_]+', recent.lower()))
            value = 1.0 if local_words & cues else 0.0
    if split_word and word.endswith('liang'):
        # Liang is the Mandarin reading of 两/兩, also seen in romanization.
        value = 3.0

    standalone_two = False
    if text in ('两', '兩'):
        value = 5.9
        standalone_two = True
    elif text == '両':
        value = 8.8
    elif text in ('俩', '倆'):
        value = 2.2
    elif any(c in text for c in '两兩両俩倆'):
        value = 5.2 if text in ('两会', '兩會') else 1.5
    elif any(c in completed for c in '両倆兩两俩'):
        value = 7.8 if '倆' in completed else 8.8
        standalone_two = any(c in completed for c in '两兩')

        # The shared byte prefix of 両 and other Han characters.
        value = 1.35
    elif text == '幾':
        value = 1.1
    elif text in ('几', '几个'):
        value = 0.4
    elif after_two:
        value += 0.8
    if len(text) >= 2 and set(text) == {'·'}:
        value = -1.1

    return (doc, (previous + raw)[-2:], word, recent, standalone_two), value

"""The Chinese numeral "two" (两 / 兩) detector for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2438.

What the component does, in plain terms:
  * It fires on the Chinese character for "two" when it is used as a quantity:
    the simplified 两 (about 5.6) and the traditional 兩 (about 6.3). These are
    its strongest responses, up to about 8.
  * It fires more weakly, about 1 to 2, on words built on that character, such as
    两个, 兩人, 两条, 这两, 两岸, which begin or contain the numeral.
  * It is slightly negative, about -1.1, on runs of middle-dot leaders (··),
    the dotted-line filler in tables of contents and forms.
  * Everything else predicts 0.

The program looks only at the current token, so it carries no state.
Other number words (English two, Spanish dos, French deux, 二) and digits are
predicted as 0; the replacement-character bytes of a split 两 are not covered.
"""

READS = ()

BARE_TWO = {"两": 5.6, "兩": 6.3}  # the numeral by itself
COMPOUND_TWO = 1.5                 # a word containing 两 or 兩
LEADER_DOTS = "··"                 # middle-dot leader
LEADER_VALUE = -1.1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token in BARE_TWO:
        value = BARE_TWO[token]
    elif "两" in token or "兩" in token:
        value = COMPOUND_TWO
    elif token == LEADER_DOTS:
        value = LEADER_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Layer-1 MLP down-projection feature 2439: a "how long ago" detector.

Its large positive responses come on the word " ago" when it closes a relative
time phrase with a short unit and a number, e.g. "3 months ago", "2 hours ago",
"4 days ago" (about +4). Without a number ("a few days ago") it is weaker (about
+1), and "years ago" / "decades ago" stay near zero. A second, rarer strong
response is the colon in a "Title:" header at the very start of a document (+5).
The first token of every document sits slightly negative (about -0.26), and the
LaTeX "array" in "\\begin{array}" gives a moderate positive (+2.5).
Everything else is predicted as 0; the component's small diffuse wobble
(about 0.05 in size) is not modelled.
"""

READS = ()

SHORT_UNITS = {"second", "seconds", "minute", "minutes", "hour", "hours", "day", "days",
               "week", "weeks", "month", "months", "día", "días", "hora", "horas",
               "mes", "meses", "semana", "semanas"}
LONG_UNITS = {"year", "years", "decade", "decades", "century", "centuries", "año", "años"}


def doc_start(prefix, i):
    """True if token i is the first token of its document within the row."""
    return (i == 0 or prefix.document_ids[i] != prefix.document_ids[i - 1]
            or prefix.token_strings[i - 1] == "<|endoftext|>")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings
    t = prefix.position
    # "Title:" as the first two tokens of a document
    if s[-1] == ":" and t >= 1 and s[-2] == "Title" and doc_start(prefix, t - 1):
        return None, 5.3
    # first token of a document
    if doc_start(prefix, t):
        return None, -0.26
    # " ago" after a duration
    if s[-1] == " ago" and t >= 1:
        unit = s[-2].strip()
        number = t >= 2 and any(ch.isdigit() for ch in s[-3])
        if unit in SHORT_UNITS:
            return None, 4.0 if number else 1.0
        if unit in LONG_UNITS:
            return None, 0.3
    # LaTeX \begin{array}
    if s[-1] == "array" and t >= 2 and s[-2] == "{" and "begin" in s[-3]:
        return None, 2.5
    return None, 0.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2440 as a readable rule set over the token stream.

The component is sparse: it is near zero on most tokens and large on a few kinds of
token. Its large activations fall into three groups, and this program predicts each.

1. Code indentation (negative). A line of code that opens with a 2-space or 4-space
   indent (or a tab then 4 spaces), the indent token coming right after a single
   newline, gives about -0.9 (-0.8 for 4 spaces). Eight spaces gives a weaker -0.25,
   a single space -0.14. If the line before ends in code punctuation such as { ; , ) the
   value is 30% larger. Blank-line breaks ("\n\n") do not count.
2. Zeros in identifiers and padding (positive).
   - A '0' right after a letter, as in v0, t0, x0, S0: +0.7.
   - A '0' that is at least the fourth zero in a row, as in 0000 padding or hashes: +0.9.
3. Two-digit numbers (positive, on the second digit): 00 +0.23, 11 +0.45, 12 +0.17,
   21 +0.37, 30 +0.38, 31 +0.32, like the days and years in dates.

Everything else predicts 0. Predictions are per token and depend only on the tokens
before it, and a rule never looks across a document boundary.
"""

READS = ()

# Indentation tokens that start a code line, and their typical activation.
INDENT = {"  ": -0.9, "    ": -0.8, "\t    ": -0.9, "        ": -0.25, " ": -0.14}
# The second digit of a two-digit number, after a first digit.
DIGIT_PAIRS = {"00": 0.23, "11": 0.45, "12": 0.17, "21": 0.37, "30": 0.38, "31": 0.32}
# Code punctuation that ends the previous line.
CODE_END = set("{};,)(\"'[]:")


def ends_with_letter(text):
    return len(text) > 0 and text[-1].isalpha()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    tok = toks[-1]
    prev = toks[-2] if len(toks) > 1 else ""
    same_doc = len(toks) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] == prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not same_doc:
        return carry, 0.0
    value = 0.0
    if tok in INDENT and prev.endswith("\n") and "\n\n" not in prev:
        code_line = prev[:-1].rstrip()[-1:] in CODE_END
        value = INDENT[tok] * (1.3 if code_line else 1.0)
    elif tok == "0" and len(toks) > 3 and toks[-2] == "0" and toks[-3] == "0" and toks[-4] == "0":
        value = 0.9
    elif prev + tok in DIGIT_PAIRS:
        value = DIGIT_PAIRS[prev + tok]
    elif tok == "0" and ends_with_letter(prev):
        value = 0.7
    return carry, value

"""Document-start detector for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2441.

What it does: this component is almost silent everywhere except at the first token of
each document. There the model has no earlier context, so the token's own identity alone
sets the activation. The program predicts a value for a document's first token only,
from what kind of token it is, and 0 at every other position.

Kinds of first token, with the value predicted for each:
- programming vocabulary (keywords, function and variable names, format strings such as
  "import", "#include", "print", "printf", "text", "name"): 9
- indentation or line breaks (whitespace only): 5
- code-like tokens (brackets, symbols, dotted names, camelCase or snake_case): 4
- capitalized English word at the start of a sentence (no leading space): 3.5
- other English words: 2.8
- special tokens such as <|im_start|>: 3.3
- non-ASCII tokens (CJK, Cyrillic, Vietnamese, emoji, ...): 1.4
- punctuation: 1.3
- digits: 0.4

A document starts at a row's first token and wherever the document label changes within
the packed row, where attention, and so this component, restarts.
"""

import re

READS = ()

PROGRAMMING_WORDS = frozenset(
    """
    include import require package using namespace return function def class struct const
    var let static public private void int char float double string bool print printf println
    echo input output scanf puts cout cin main self this new null nil true false none len
    range append list dict array map set get put value key name text data file path test
    error log config options args result index count size length id url html div span
    script style button label title form table row item items element node parent callback
    event query select insert update delete create model view user username password email
    token request response json xml str sizeof malloc free fopen fclose fgets fread fwrite
    """.split()
)

CODE_LIKE = re.compile(r"[_$#{}()\[\];=<>\\@/\"]|\.[A-Za-z]|[a-z][A-Z]|\t")
ENGLISH_WORD = re.compile(r" ?[A-Za-z]+")


def kind_value(token: str) -> float:
    bare = token.strip().lower().strip("_.$#(\"'\t")
    if bare in PROGRAMMING_WORDS:
        return 9.0
    if token.startswith("<|") and token.endswith("|>"):
        return 3.3
    if any(ord(ch) > 127 for ch in token):
        return 1.4
    if token.strip() == "":
        return 5.0
    if token.strip().isdigit():
        return 0.4
    if CODE_LIKE.search(token):
        return 4.0
    if ENGLISH_WORD.fullmatch(token):
        return 3.5 if token[0].isupper() else 2.8
    return 1.3


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict this component's activation at the newest position of the prefix."""
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not starts_document:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, float(kind_value(prefix.token_strings[-1]))

"""Link-target detector for layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2443, with two weak extras.

Plain-language reading: this component responds to where a link target begins, and
whether the target is an outside web address or a local place.

- The "://" that completes a URL scheme ("http://", "https://") gives a strong negative
  value, about -1.5. This is the component's clearest and largest response.
- Inside a Markdown link "](...)", the first token of the target gives a positive value
  when it opens an in-page anchor ("#", about +1.3) or a site-relative path ("/", about +0.9).
- Weak extras: the first token of a packed row is slightly negative (about -0.12), and a
  slash joining two prose words ("pins/pads") is slightly positive (about +0.2).
- Every other position predicts 0. Most tokens have small, token-specific activations
  that no simple rule captures, so 0 is the best guess for them.

On the eval rows this explains about 9.5% of the variance (r = 0.31). The URL and
link-target rules alone give about 8%. The rest is spread over many small values, and
the program's e2e effect on the model's output is about the same as switching the
component off.
"""

READS = ()

SCHEMES = ("http", "https")
ANCHOR_OR_PATH = {"#": 1.3, "/": 0.9}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix) > 1 else ""

What it does, in plain terms: this component is almost silent everywhere except on the
FIRST token of a document (the token right after a document boundary, where the model
has no earlier context). There it switches on or off according to what kind of token
opens the document:

  * a space followed by LaTeX maths or inline code (" $", " `", " \\(")  -> strongly positive
  * a space followed by an opening bracket, operator or code symbol (" (", " =", " [", " <")

  * the same symbols with no leading space                                  -> mildly positive
  * Chinese characters                                                     -> mildly positive
  * imperative / task verbs that start an instruction ("Use", "Create",
    "Develop", "Design", "Making", ...)                                    -> positive
  * articles, pronouns and prepositions ("The", "the", "A", "I", "They",
    "to", "of", ...)                                                       -> negative
  * digits and closing brackets / punctuation                              -> slightly negative
  * anything else                                                          -> near the mean (+0.2)

text, so the program is a readable approximation of the component's activation, not an
exact one: within each group the real activation still varies a lot.

It explains roughly 18% of the activation variance on the eval rows; most of the
remaining variance is idiosyncratic per-token behaviour at document starts, which a token
table would capture better but which has no clean concept behind it.

VERBS = set("""use create make build design develop implement configure install manage add
write generate construct consider find get set define run call learn click explain describe
provide know understand enable support handle process apply check convert calculate compute
print show display read load save update delete remove insert select perform improve identify
determine collect deploy test start stop open close send receive join follow include making
adding using creating building designing developing implementing configuring installing managing
running calling learning writing generating constructing considering finding getting setting
defining providing knowing understanding enabling supporting handling processing applying
checking converting calculating computing printing showing displaying reading loading saving
updating deleting removing inserting selecting performing improving identifying determining
collecting testing starting stopping opening closing sending receiving joining
following including""".split())

def doc_start_value(tok):
    """Predicted activation for a token that is the first of its document."""
    core = tok.strip()
    if not core or core.startswith("<|"):  # special tokens such as <|im_start|>
        return 0.0
    if tok.startswith(" ") and re.match(r"[$`]|\\\(", core):
        return 11.0  # a space, then LaTeX maths or inline code
    if tok.startswith(" ") and core[0] in "([<=\\'":
        return 3.8  # a space, then an opening bracket, operator or quote
    if core[0] in "([{<$`\\=\"'" or core in ('"""', "/*", "#!/"):
        return 1.8  # the same symbols without a leading space
    if re.search(r"[一-鿿]", core):

    if core.lower() in VERBS:

"""Layer 1, MLP down_proj component 2445: a weak, mostly diffuse signal.

What it does, in plain terms:
  * Its activation is near zero almost everywhere, with small token-to-token noise. This
    program predicts only the parts that recur:

    negative when it is a word (about -0.17), near zero otherwise.
  * Words of self-checking, hedging or requesting ("please", "again", "think", "error",
    "mistake", "carefully", "perhaps", "maybe", "verify", "helpful", "detailed") lean
    slightly negative (about -0.05), and more so when such words recur in the last few tokens
    (a reflective or hedging stretch of text).
  * Comparison and quantity words ("more", "less", "further", "much", "than", "higher",
    "little", "lot") and modal or auxiliary verbs ("could", "would", "will", "shall", "were",
    "going", "can", "are") lean slightly positive (about +0.05 and +0.03).
  * Everything else predicts 0.

1-2% of the activation's variance; the component's effect on the model's output is tiny.

READS = ()

HEDGE_OR_REQUEST = {
    "please", "provide", "again", "think", "error", "errors", "mistake", "carefully",
    "perhaps", "maybe", "verify", "helpful", "detailed", "accurate", "sure", "description",
}
COMPARISON = {"more", "less", "further", "much", "than", "higher", "lower", "little", "lot"}
MODAL_OR_AUX = {"could", "would", "will", "shall", "were", "going", "can", "are"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if prefix.position == 0:
        return carry, (-0.17 if text.strip().isalpha() else 0.0)
    word = text.strip().lower()

        return carry, -0.05
    if word in COMPARISON:
        return carry, 0.05

What it does (plain terms). Layer 1's MLP writes this component into the residual
stream, and it is nearly silent on ordinary text. It switches on where text spells
characters out as escapes or as broken bytes:

1. Hex byte escapes of UTF-8 characters, as in "\xe2\x80\x99" (a curly apostrophe).
   The lead byte fires hardest: "\xe" (3-byte lead) about 8, "\xc" (2-byte lead) about
   3.5. Continuation bytes "\x8" to "\xb" fire about 2.2, and the second hex digit
   of a byte fires about 0.9 after a lead byte, 0.45 after a continuation byte.
   When the backslash sits in an earlier token (a bare "xe"), it fires about 1.5x more.
2. Other backslash escapes: an escaped apostrophe "\'" (5.5), "\"", "\n", "\t", "\r"
   (about 1.2). The letter after a bare backslash, as in LaTeX "\left" or "\text", about 0.8.
3. HTML character references: "&#" (6), and "&amp", "&gt", "&lt", "&quot" (1.5).
4. Mojibake: a UTF-8 lead byte read as Latin-1, such as "â" in "doesnâ€™t" or "Ã" (4.5).
   A stray replacement character "�" in otherwise ASCII text gets 1.5.
5. A literal backslash-n typed into English prose (" \n" after a word) is negative,
   about -1; after a space alone, -0.4.

Everything else predicts 0. The program reads only the newest token and the decoded
text so far (its last four characters), so it needs no carry between positions.
"""

import re

READS = ()

HEX_TAIL = re.compile(r"\\x([0-9a-fA-F]{0,2})$")    # text ends in \x, \xN or \xNN
ESCAPE_LETTER = re.compile(r"\\[nrt\"/dv]")         # a token holding \n, \", \t, ...
PROSE_WORD = re.compile(r" ?[A-Za-z]{2,}[.,;:]?$")  # an English word, as before a "\n"
MOJIBAKE_LEAD = {"â", "Ã", " â", " Ã", "€™", "\x92"}
HTML_NAMED = {"&gt", "&lt", "&quot", "&amp"}


def _lead_byte(first_digit: str) -> float:
    """Activation when a byte's first hex digit is typed: \\e is a 3-byte lead."""
    if first_digit == "e":
        return 8.0
    if first_digit in "cdf":
        return 3.5
    return 2.2  # 8, 9, a, b: continuation bytes


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.text_prefixes[-1][-4:]
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""

    m = HEX_TAIL.search(text)
    if m:
        digits = m.group(1)
        if digits == "":  # the backslash-x has just been typed
            value = 2.3
        elif len(digits) == 1:  # first hex digit of the byte
            value = _lead_byte(digits)
            if not tok.startswith("\\"):  # the backslash came in an earlier token
                value *= 1.5
        else:  # second hex digit of the byte
            value = 0.9 if digits[0] in "cdef" else 0.45
    elif tok == "\\'":
        value = 5.5
    elif "&#" in tok:
        value = 6.0
    elif tok in HTML_NAMED:
        value = 1.5
    elif tok in MOJIBAKE_LEAD:
        value = 4.5
    elif tok == " \\":  # a literal \n typed after a word is negative; after a space less so
        value = -1.0 if PROSE_WORD.search(prev) else (-0.4 if prev.strip() == "" else 0.0)
    elif ESCAPE_LETTER.search(tok):
        value = 1.2
    elif "\\" in tok:
        value = 0.0
    elif prev.endswith("\\") and tok[:1].isalpha():  # the letter after a bare backslash
        value = 0.8
    elif tok == "\ufffd":  # a stray replacement character after ASCII text
        value = 1.5 if prev and all(ord(c) < 128 for c in prev) else 0.1
    elif "\ufffd" in tok:
        value = 0.1
    elif tok == "\x00":  # UTF-16 text, one null byte per character
        value = 1.2
    elif tok in ("`", " `"):
        value = 0.35
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Approximate a rare response to English with lowercase a's dropped out.

A document-local text window checks for missing a's and damaged function
words. Frequency-weighted dictionary prefixes then identify the current
word fragment as a possible a-deleted spelling. Most text gets a small
baseline. Middle-dot leaders have a separate positive response.
"""
from collections import defaultdict
from functools import lru_cache
import re
from wordfreq import top_n_list, zipf_frequency

READS = ()
ENGLISH = set('the of to is in for with this be on we if it'.split())
FUNCTION_WORDS = set(
    'and are any that than can has had have was what all also about after'.split()
)
DAMAGED = {word.replace('a', '') for word in FUNCTION_WORDS}
NORMAL = defaultdict(float)
OMITTED = defaultdict(float)
EXACT = {}
for word in top_n_list('en', 30000):
    if not word.isascii() or not word.isalpha():
        continue
    weight = 10 ** (0.45 * (zipf_frequency(word, 'en') - 4))
    EXACT[word] = weight
    for n in range(1, len(word) + 1):
        NORMAL[word[:n]] += weight
    if 'a' in word:
        damaged = word.replace('a', '')
        for n in range(1, len(damaged) + 1):
            OMITTED[damaged[:n]] += weight


@lru_cache(maxsize=100000)
def spelling_evidence(word):
    ordinary = NORMAL.get(word, 0.)
    damaged = OMITTED.get(word, 0.)
    prefix_ratio = damaged / (ordinary + damaged + 1e-6)
    repaired = max(
        EXACT.get(word[:i] + 'a' + word[i:], 0.)
        for i in range(len(word) + 1)
    )
    repair_ratio = repaired / (EXACT.get(word, 0.) + repaired + 1e-6)
    return prefix_ratio, repair_ratio


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    text = '' if carry is None or carry[0] != doc else carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    text = (text + token)[-400:]
    carry = (doc, text)
    if len(token) >= 2 and not token.strip('·'):
        return carry, 1.37
    match = re.search('[A-Za-z]+$', text)
    word = match.group().lower() if match else ''
    if not word or 'a' in word:
        return carry, 0.0024

    letters = ''.join(ch for ch in text if 'a' <= ch <= 'z')[-160:]
    missing = max(0., 1. - letters.count('a') / max(1., len(letters) * .035))
    missing *= min(1., len(letters) / 90.)
    words = re.findall('[a-z]+', text.lower())
    english = min(1., sum(w in ENGLISH for w in words) / 5.)
    damage = min(1., sum(w in DAMAGED for w in words) / 2.)
    mode = missing * english * damage
    if text.count(';') >= 3 or '>>' in text or '<<' in text:
        mode = 0.
    if mode == 0.:
        return carry, 0.0024
    p, r = spelling_evidence(word)
    value = 0.0024 - mode * (2.9 * p + 1.37 * r)
    return carry, value

"""Layer-1 MLP down-projection component 2447: a document-start detector.

What it does, in plain terms: the component is almost silent inside a
document. Its clearest behaviour is at the first token of each document
(the packed rows restart at each document, so the model sees that token
with no context at all). There it takes a sign set by the kind of token:

* ALL-CAPS identifier pieces (e.g. "_TOTAL", "FACT", "CTION") go negative;
* digits, bare whitespace, and a space followed by punctuation
  (e.g. " |", ' "') go positive.

Everything else, and every position after the first token, predicts 0.
The rules are a rough summary; the exact per-token values are idiosyncratic.
"""

import re

READS = ()

ALL_CAPS = re.compile(r"[A-Z_0-9]*[A-Z][A-Z_0-9]*")
VALUE_CAPS = -0.3
VALUE_OPEN = 0.3


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    body = text.strip()
    starts_document = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not starts_document:
        return None, 0.0
    if len(body) > 1 and ALL_CAPS.fullmatch(body):
        return None, VALUE_CAPS
    if body.isdigit() or body == "" or (text[:1] == " " and not body[:1].isalnum()):
        return None, VALUE_OPEN
    return None, 0.0

"""Layer 1, MLP down-projection, component 2449: a sparse "unit / file-format suffix" detector.

What it does: this component is silent almost everywhere (it passes the causal-importance
threshold on about 0.04% of tokens). When it does fire, it is strongly negative on the
token that completes a short technical name made from a prefix letter plus a unit or
format, for example:

  * "mp3", "mp4", "MPa": the digit (or "a") right after "mp" (MP3/MP4 media files, MPa)
  * "kPa", "KPa", "GPa", "hPa": the "Pa" (pascal) after a metric prefix letter
  * "kbytes": "bytes" after "k"
  * "mph", "kmph": the "ph" after "km" / "k" / "M"
  * "匹" (the Chinese counter for horses, as in "8匹马")
  * the "-" in a diff/patch hunk header "@@ -4,7 +4,7 @@"

Everything else is predicted as 0. The rules are chosen from the largest activations in
training text; the magnitudes are the typical activations for each rule. It is a
readable approximation: the full activation has a long tail of small, context-specific
values that these few rules do not capture (roughly 0.10 variance explained on eval).
"""

READS = ()

SI_PREFIXES = ("k", "K", "G", "M", "h")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix) > 1 else ""
    before = prev.strip()

    # MP3 / MP4 / MPa: the digit or "a" right after "mp" (any case).
    if (cur.isdigit() or cur == "a") and before.lower().endswith("mp"):
        return None, -7.0
    # kPa, KPa, GPa, hPa, MPa: the pascal unit after a metric prefix letter.
    if cur in ("Pa", "PA", "pa", "PI") and before in SI_PREFIXES:
        return None, -4.5
    # mph / kmph: the "ph" after km, k or M.
    if cur == "ph" and before in ("km", "k", "M"):
        return None, -3.5
    # kbytes: "bytes" after "k".
    if cur == "bytes" and before == "k":
        return None, -2.5
    # 匹, the counter for horses ("8匹馬").
    if cur == "匹":
        return None, -4.0
    # "-" opening the old-range of a diff hunk header "@@ -4,7 +4,7 @@".
    if cur == " -" and prev == "@@":
        return None, -1.4
    return None, 0.0


class _Prefix:

"""Digits inside alphanumeric names and codes: the number that follows a capital-letter
stem in product, gene, part or model names (TLR7, STK33, SV40, MGC803, IR2104, GS-04B, DXC-950).

It reads the text just before each token, back to the last space, and fires when that text
ends in a letter stem (optionally followed by one hyphen) and the token continues the code:
- a hyphen right after a stem of two or more capitals (GS-, XC-, AA-): 1.35;
- the first digit after an all-capital stem (TLR7, AA-7): 0.2 after one capital, 1.2 after
  two, 1.4 after three;
- a later digit of the same code (IR21|0, MGC80|3, hsc7|0): 1.2 after one capital, 2.5 after
  two, 2.4 after three; 0.5 after a lowercase stem (hsc70), 1.0 after a mixed-case stem.
It predicts 0 everywhere else: ordinary numbers (after a space, in lists, years, prices,
dates), digits after a hyphen that follows digits (0-03-81), and all other tokens.
The values are mean activations on training text, in the component's own units.
"""

READS = ()

import re

DIGITS = "0123456789"
FIRST = {0: 0.0, 1: 0.2, 2: 1.2, 3: 1.4}      # first digit after an all-caps stem, by capitals
LATER = {0: 0.5, 1: 1.2, 2: 2.5, 3: 2.4}     # a later digit of the code, by capitals


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    n = len(prefix.token_ids)
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if tok not in DIGITS and tok != "-":
        return carry, 0.0
    # the text before this token, back to the start of this document (at most 40 tokens)
    start = n - 1
    while start > 0 and n - start < 40 and prefix.document_ids[start - 1] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        start -= 1
    before = "".join(prefix.token_strings[start : n - 1])
    word = re.search(r"\S*$", before).group(0)
    run = word.rstrip(DIGITS)               # the word without the digits right before this token
    earlier = len(word) - len(run)          # digits of this code before this token
    if tok == "-":
        if earlier:                         # a hyphen after digits: a number, not a code
            return carry, 0.0
    elif run.endswith("-"):
        run = run[:-1]                      # the stem sits before one hyphen (GS-04)
        if not run[-1:].isalpha():
            return carry, 0.0
    stem = re.search(r"[A-Za-z]*$", run).group(0)
    caps = min(sum(c.isupper() for c in stem), 3)
    lows = sum(c.islower() for c in stem)
    if tok == "-":
        return carry, (1.35 if caps >= 2 and lows == 0 else 0.0)
    if caps == 0 and lows == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    if earlier:                             # this digit follows other digits of the code
        if lows == 0:
            return carry, LATER[caps]
        return carry, 0.5 if caps == 0 else 1.0
    if lows == 0:
        return carry, FIRST[caps]
    return carry, 0.0

"""Recognize unusual spacing at UTF-8 token boundaries.

The last byte of an EM SPACE is strongly positive, especially when it is
novel in otherwise ordinary text. Recent non-ASCII spaces and characters
reduce that response. Middle-dot separators and nonbreaking spaces have
smaller positive responses, as do unfinished UTF-8 continuations.
Most text stays near zero; other character-specific spikes are not modeled.
"""
import codecs
import math
from collections import deque

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        position, pending, recent = 0, b'', deque(maxlen=64)
    else:
        _, position, pending, recent = carry
    raw = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    decoder = codecs.getincrementaldecoder('utf-8')('replace')
    decoder.setstate((pending, 0))
    text = decoder.decode(raw)
    remaining = decoder.getstate()[0]
    value = 0.002
    if raw == b'\x83' and text == '\u2003':
        context = ''.join(recent)
        unusual_spaces = sum(c.isspace() and ord(c) > 127 for c in context)
        non_ascii = sum(ord(c) > 127 for c in context)
        whitespace = sum(c.isspace() for c in context) / max(1, len(context))
        value = (3.0 + 1.5 / math.sqrt(1 + position / 16)
                 - 0.44 * math.log1p(unusual_spaces)
                 - 0.43 * math.log1p(non_ascii) + 0.94 * whitespace)
        value = max(0.5, value)
        if not context:
            value = 6.2
    elif text == '··':
        value = 0.54
    elif text == '\u00a0':
        value = 0.08
    elif (len(raw) == 1 and 0x80 <= raw[0] < 0xc0
          and len(remaining) == 2):
        value = 0.25
    recent.append(text)
    return (doc, position + 1, remaining, recent), value

"""Layer 1 MLP down-projection component 2454: a split-character detector.

Qwen's byte-level tokenizer sometimes splits one character across tokens. The first
tokens of such a character decode alone to U+FFFD, and the token that finally completes
the character is where this component speaks. Its size and sign depend on which
character is completed, not on the byte-level tokens as such. Measured on training text,
it is near zero everywhere else.

The program: when the current token completes a character, it predicts that character's
typical activation from a table of the characters that move the component most (measured
on about 8 million training tokens). Everywhere else it predicts 0.

Strongly negative: the C1 control characters U+0083, U+008E, U+008F (bytes C2 83, C2 8E,
C2 8F), U+E103, U+0943 and a few rare CJK characters. Strongly positive: EM SPACE U+2003
(bytes E2 80 83) and a few rare CJK characters.
"""

READS = ()

# Mean activation when this character is completed by its last byte.
COMPLETED_CHAR_ACTIVATION = {
    "\u0083": -6.1,  # bytes C2 83 (U+0083)
    "\u008e": -5.8,  # bytes C2 8E (U+008E)
    "\u008f": -3.1,  # bytes C2 8F (U+008F)
    "\u2003": 2.5,  # EM SPACE, bytes E2 80 83
    "\ue103": -3.6,  # private use, bytes EE 84 83
    "\u0943": -6.4,  # Devanagari vowel sign II, bytes E0 A5 83
    "\u9283": 2.5,  # rare CJK character
    "\u685c": -3.5,  # rare CJK character
    "\u68f2": -3.2,  # rare CJK character
    "\u54b2": -2.7,  # rare CJK character
    "\u9234": 1.25,  # rare CJK character
    "\u6afb": -1.6,  # rare CJK character
    "\u9b8e": -0.9,  # rare CJK character
    "\u5ec3": 1.0,  # rare CJK character
    "\u5e81": 1.2,  # rare CJK character
    "\u6158": -1.1,  # rare CJK character
    "\u4e3c": 1.0,  # rare CJK character
}

REPLACEMENT = "\ufffd"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.token_strings[t] != REPLACEMENT:
        return carry, 0.0  # only a partial-character token can complete a character
    if prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    now = prefix.text_prefixes[t]
    before = prefix.text_prefixes[t - 1]
    if now[-1:] == REPLACEMENT or not before.endswith(REPLACEMENT):
        return carry, 0.0  # this token did not complete a character
    return carry, float(COMPLETED_CHAR_ACTIVATION.get(now[-1], 0.0))

classifier gives a negative response. Modifier and noun-class strengths

possibly before a Japanese particle. Short byte history handles split characters.

with each document.

    ('该該', 3.27),  # that/aforesaid
    ('各', 1.0),  # each/all
    ('每毎', 1.09),  # every

    ('当當', 1.44),  # at/current
    ('这這', 0.24),  # this
    ('那', 0.29),  # that
    ('哪', 1.11),  # which
    ('此', 0.98),  # this

    ('同', 1.7),  # same
    ('上', 0.15),  # previous
    ('下', 0.71),  # next

    (1.28, '年 年度'),  # year
    (1.63, '学期 學期 期 季度 世纪 世紀 阶段 階段 节课 節課'),  # time spans / phases
    (1.5, '国 國 市 省 县 縣 区 區'),  # territory

    (0.4, '项 項 部门 部門 人 位 篇文章 刻 届 屆'),  # other counted nouns

Plain-terms summary. This component is silent almost everywhere. It goes negative in two
situations, and the size of the dip depends on the token that is there:

1. The first token of a document. A document starts at the beginning of a row and after
   every <|endoftext|> boundary (the model resets attention there). With no context to look
   at, the response is set by the token alone:
   - a bare digit (0-9, one token) dips hard, about -1.6;
   - a word in a non-CJK, non-Latin-ASCII script (Cyrillic, Thai, Greek, accented Latin, ...)
     dips about -1.2;
   - an ASCII fragment or punctuation with no leading space dips about -0.5;
   - a CJK character dips slightly, about -0.15;
   - a word with a leading space is near zero, about -0.1.

2. Chinese and Japanese scope words that begin with a determiner-like character meaning
   "this", "each", "every", "local", "current", "the said" (本 当 各 每 该 今 此). Examples
   that fire: 本站 (this site), 当地 (local), 各地 (various places), 每年 (every year),
   该案 (this case), 今年 (this year). They dip about -0.5. The same characters are not
   negative for 这 (this) or 某 (some), so the rule is not "any determiner".

Everywhere else the program predicts 0. The residual variance is diffuse, small, and not
explained by any simple word class.

The program is stateless: it reads only the newest token and whether it starts a document.
"""

# Chinese/Japanese scope determiners: this, local, each, every, the said, current, this (ci).

    return char.isalpha() and 0x2E80 <= ord(char) <= 0x9FFF

    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]  # the newest token, decoded alone
    word = raw.strip()
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]

    if starts_document:
        if word.isdigit():
            return None, -1.6
        if word and not word.isascii() and word[0].isalpha() and not is_cjk(word[0]):
            return None, -1.2
        if word and is_cjk(word[0]):
            return None, -0.15

        return None, -0.5

        return None, -0.5
    return None, 0.0

"""Spelling-based approximation: short f syllables, plus 'of course'.

Short fo/foc/fol pieces tend negative; vowel+r pieces tend positive.
A syllable split across tokens generally has a larger response. Longer
completed words mostly get zero. A fixed transliteration table extends the
same spelling rules to other scripts; these are not semantic word classes.
The only memory is the preceding token, reset at document boundaries.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
from anyascii import anyascii

READS = ()

# Ordered spelling families: name, full-match pattern, within-token response,
# across-token response. The explicit or/oun exclusion leaves common longer
# forms such as 'form', 'force', and 'found' unmarked.
RULES = (
    ('air', r'[oa]ir(?:s|e)?', .306, 2.333),
    ('ir_ur', r'[iuy]r(?:s|t|th)?', .884, 2.504),
    ('ort', r'orts?', 1.444, 2.275),
    ('or', r'or(?:us|um|a|ia)?', -.009, .835),
    ('exclude', r'(?:or|oun).*', 0., 0.),
    ('ar', r'ar(?:s|n|si)?', .007, .803),
    ('ine', r'ine', .068, .348),
    ('ant', r'ant', .036, 1.797),
    ('other_r', r'(?:hir|r[wu])', .183, 3.404),
    ('short_o', r'o(?:[lnstgckdbf]|ci|cal|ld|lds)?', -2.203, -3.572),
    ('long_ol', r'(?:old|oll|olk|oly).*', -.843, -1.769),
    ('focus', r'(?:ocus|okus).*', -.627, -1.177),
    ('double_o', r'oo.*', -.913, -1.012),
    ('long_o', r'o(?:nt|nd|ne|to|no|ni|en).*', -.278, -.935),
    ('other_o', r'o.{0,3}', -.142, -.806),
    ('closed_a', r'a(?:x|ch|l|ld|lm|d|de|der|sh|g|p|j|y)', -1.359, -2.101),
    ('other_closed', r'(?:il|um|us|itch|ifo)', -.243, -1.190),
    ('weak_vowel', r'(?:a|u|e|en|ag|age|ages)', -.031, -.577),
)


@lru_cache(maxsize=32768)
def spelling(text):
    return anyascii(text).lower()


@lru_cache(maxsize=32768)
def family(tail):
    for name, pattern, inside, split in RULES:
        if re.fullmatch(pattern, tail):
            return name, inside, split
    return '', 0., 0.


@lru_cache(maxsize=32768)
def after_f(text):
    """Letters after the final f or ph spelling, if nothing intervenes."""
    matches = list(re.finditer(r'f|ph', text))
    if not matches:
        return None
    tail = text[matches[-1].end():]
    return tail if tail.isalpha() or not tail else None

    t, old = spelling(token), spelling(previous)
    if t.strip() == 'course' and old.strip() in ('of', 'off'):

        return 10.8 if previous.strip()[:1].isupper() else 8.7

    start = re.fullmatch(r'[^a-z]*f([a-z]+)', t)
    if start:
        tail = start.group(1)
        name, value, _ = family(tail)
        # Separate short fragments from their longer completed word forms.
        if ((name == 'air' and tail != 'air')
                or (name == 'ir_ur' and not token.isascii())
                or (name == 'double_o' and tail != 'oo')
                or (name == 'long_ol' and tail not in ('olding', 'olded'))):
            value = 0.0
    remainder = after_f(old)
    if (remainder is not None and len(remainder) <= 2
            and t and t[0].isalpha()):

        if name == 'ine' and old.endswith('ph'):

        value += split
    return value

    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    previous = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ''
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    return (doc, token), float(predict(previous, token))

and verb endings (" bir", " bu", "-cek", "-ır"), and on a degenerate run of
dot-leader filler tokens ("··").

counted from the document's start, and the document counts as Turkish once it
has five such hits.

# (possessive and case endings, typically 5 to 10 in a Turkish document) ...

                  "inden", "ından", "den", "dan", "ın", "sin", "kin", "'n", "’in",
                  "ları", "larını", "ların", "lara", "aya", "una", "yle", "izin",
                  "ye", "ince"}
# ... and weaker ones (typically about 1.5).

                "adan", "eye", "eden", "’a", "’"}
# Turkish postpositions and particles, written with a leading space.
SPACED_WEAK = {" da", " hakkında", " üzerinden", " ile", " ya"}

NEGATIVE_WORDS = {" bir", " bö", " bu", " ol", "cek", "iz", "ır", "lar", "ur"}

WEAK_VALUE = 1.5
NEG_VALUE = -2.0

"""Mostly an East Asian line-boundary signal, strongest in Chinese text.

Count scripts in the last 128 decoded characters of the current document.
At a newline, scale a punctuation-dependent response by the fraction of
East Asian versus ASCII letters. Japanese and Korean contexts usually
respond less.
Code delimiters stay quiet. Repeated middle dots, a typographic leader,
have a separate negative response.
Other lexical variation is deliberately left unexplained.
"""
import regex

READS = ()
HAN = regex.compile(r'\p{Script=Han}')
KANA = regex.compile(r'[\p{Script=Hiragana}\p{Script=Katakana}]')
HANGUL = regex.compile(r'\p{Script=Hangul}')

# Columns: Chinese, Japanese, Korean context.
RESPONSE = {
    'line': (0.79, 0.29, 0.07),
    'blank': (0.99, 0.36, 0.06),
    'paragraph': (0.25, 0.27, 0.08),
    'period': (0.35, 0.08, 0.00),
    'cjk_punctuation': (0.44, 0.28, 0.00),
    'punctuation': (0.55, 0.20, 0.08),
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    first = carry is None or carry[0] != doc
    text = '' if first else carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = 0.0
    if '\n' in token and not any(c in token for c in '{};='):
        han = len(HAN.findall(text))
        kana = len(KANA.findall(text))
        hangul = len(HANGUL.findall(text))
        eastern = han + kana + hangul
        latin = sum(c.isascii() and c.isalpha() for c in text)
        if eastern >= 3:
            language = 1 if kana >= 3 else 2 if hangul >= 3 else 0
            punctuation = token.strip()
            if token.count('\n') > 1:
                kind = 'paragraph' if punctuation else 'blank'
            elif not punctuation:
                kind = 'line'
            elif '。' in punctuation:
                kind = 'period'
            elif any(c in punctuation for c in '，、…）'):
                kind = 'cjk_punctuation'
            else:
                kind = 'punctuation'
            value = RESPONSE[kind][language] * eastern / (eastern + latin)
    if len(token) >= 2 and not token.strip('·'):
        value = -0.93
    return (doc, (text + token)[-128:]), value

"""Line breaks inside Chinese-language text (layers.1.mlp.down_proj, component 2463).

What the component does, in plain terms:
  * It mostly stays silent. It only responds to a newline token ("\n", "\n\n", "。\n", ")\n", ...).
  * A newline responds in proportion to how Chinese the surrounding document is so far:
    the share of this document's tokens so far that are Chinese characters or Chinese
    punctuation (tracked from the start of the document). A newline in an English
    or code document gives about 0; a newline in a fully Chinese document gives about 0.6.
  * The first token of each document (where the model's attention can only see
    itself) gives a small negative value, about -0.12.

Everything else predicts 0. Predicting the rule above explains roughly 7% of the
component's variance on held-out text; the tail is spread over many ordinary tokens.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

NEWLINE_GAIN = 0.6  # newline activation per unit of Chinese share
DOC_START = -0.12  # activation on the first token of a document


def is_chinese(token: str) -> bool:
    """True if the token holds a CJK ideograph, CJK punctuation or a fullwidth character."""
    return any(
        "一" <= c <= "鿿" or "　" <= c <= "〿" or "＀" <= c <= "￯"
        for c in token
    )


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    # carry: (Chinese tokens so far in this document, all tokens so far in this document)
    chinese, total = (0, 0) if new_doc or carry is None else carry
    chinese += is_chinese(token)
    total += 1
    share = chinese / total  # Chinese share of this document so far, counting this token
    value = NEWLINE_GAIN * share if "\n" in token else 0.0
    if new_doc:
        value += DOC_START
    return (chinese, total), value

"""A coarse document-onset and spelling-shape approximation.

The strongest broad pattern is a negative contribution on a document's
first token, especially alphabetic tokens. After a brief dip, the average
slowly rises toward a small positive value. Away from document onset,
alphabetic forms get a positive adjustment, reduced for common English
words and longer tokens. ASCII tokens and tokens decoded with replacement
characters receive small adjustments. This does not explain the remaining token-specific variation.
"""
import math
from functools import lru_cache
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

READS = ()


@lru_cache(maxsize=32768)
def spelling_bias(token):
    text = token.strip()
    alphabetic = text.isalpha()
    bias = -0.0019 * len(text)
    if token.isascii():
        bias += 0.020
    if "\ufffd" in text:
        bias += 0.038
    if alphabetic:
        bias += 0.0345 - 0.00415 * zipf_frequency(text.lower(), "en")
    return bias, alphabetic


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    position = carry[1] + 1 if carry and carry[0] == document else 0
    n = position + 1
    value = (0.001 - 0.174 / math.sqrt(n) + 0.222 / n
             - 0.00063 * math.log(n))
    bias, alphabetic = spelling_bias(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    value += bias
    if position == 0:
        value -= 0.183 + 0.1293 * alphabetic
    elif position == 1:
        value -= 0.0145
    return (document, position), value

"""Approximate the component's Romance-prose word-piece responses.

Recent common words give a rough language guess. At word starts, selected
function-word spellings get negative values. Some Latin-prefix-like spellings
get positive values unless they are frequent whole words. Likely mathematical
uses of `sin` are skipped. These are spelling tests, not semantic judgments of
negation. Japanese responses and many individual lexical preferences remain
unmodeled. State resets when the document label changes.

import re
from functools import lru_cache
from wordfreq import top_n_list, zipf_frequency

READS = ()
# Extra Latin-script languages keep non-Romance prose from triggering rules.
LANGUAGES = (
    'en', 'fr', 'es', 'pt', 'it', 'ro', 'de', 'nl', 'sv', 'da', 'nb',
    'fi', 'hu', 'tr', 'pl', 'cs', 'sk', 'ca', 'sh', 'id', 'vi',
)
COMMON_WORDS = set().union(*(set(top_n_list(l, 100)) for l in LANGUAGES))
MATH_WORDS = set('sin cos tan log exp frac sqrt theta alpha beta gamma pi'.split())
AD_FORMS = {'ac', 'ad', 'af', 'ag', 'al', 'an', 'ap', 'ar', 'as', 'at'}
LATIN_PREFIXES = ('re', 'pre', 'pro', 'co', 'de', 'ex', 'en', 'em', 'in',
                  'im', 'ab', 'sub', 'sup', 'per', 'es')

@lru_cache(None)
def evidence(word):
    if word not in COMMON_WORDS or word in MATH_WORDS:
        return None
    fs = [zipf_frequency(word, lang) for lang in LANGUAGES]
    mean = sum(fs) / len(fs)
    return tuple(f - mean for f in fs)


def advance(carry, text, document):
    if carry is None or carry[0] != document:
        carry = (document, (2.,) + (0.,) * (len(LANGUAGES) - 1), '', '')
    _, scores, word, recent = carry
    for part in re.findall(r'[^\W\d_]+|[\W\d_]+', text):
        if part.isalpha():
            word += part.lower()
        else:
            ev = evidence(word) if 2 <= len(word) <= 20 else None
            if ev is not None:
                scores = tuple(.93 * a + b for a, b in zip(scores, ev))
            word = ''
    return document, scores, word, (recent + text)[-64:]


# Selected short function-word spellings; these are not semantic classifiers.
FUNCTION_WORDS = {
    # nor, without, if, not, because, negative "point"
    'fr': {'ni': -3.6, 'sans': -2.4, 'si': -1.6, 'sí': -1.6,
           'non': -1.2, 'car': -3.1, 'point': -2.9},
    # nor, without, if / affirmative "yes"
    'es': {'ni': -3.6, 'sin': -3.6, 'si': -2.0, 'sí': -2.0},
    # nor, without, if
    'pt': {'nem': -3.6, 'sem': -2.9, 'se': -0.3},
    # without, if, not
    'it': {'senza': -1.3, 'se': -0.7, 'non': -0.5},
}

def response(text, language, previous):
    word = text.strip().lstrip("'’").lower()
    starts_word = (text[:1].isspace() or text.startswith(("'", '’')) or
                   not previous or not previous[-1].isalpha())

            not word.isalpha() or not starts_word):

    math_context = r'[=^\\_$]|\b(sin|cos|tan|frac|theta)\b'
    if word == 'sin' and re.search(math_context, previous[-40:]):

    # Latin ad- assimilates to ac-, ap-, ar-, etc. before consonants.
    prefix = (word.startswith(LATIN_PREFIXES) or
              word[:2] in AD_FORMS or word == 'é')

    language = LANGUAGES[winner] if scores[winner] > scores[0] + 1. else 'en'
    return carry, float(response(text, language, previous))

"""Approximate an orthographic ch/che feature, not a semantic topic.

Follow the unfinished word across token boundaries. Distinguish short vowel
continuations of ch, consonant continuations of che, and ch already inside
a token. Repeated ch is usually negative. Check and achieve are separate
spelling families. The small table calibrates these named patterns, case
and non-ASCII letters; there is no token-identity lookup.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
from math import sqrt

import regex
from anyascii import anyascii

READS = ()
TAIL = re.compile('[a-z]+$')
HAN = regex.compile(r'\p{Script=Han}')
# Pattern: base strength, uppercase adjustment, non-ASCII-letter adjustment.
STRENGTH = {
    'none':          (-0.002,  0.000,  0.000),
    'che':           (0.598,  0.901, -0.302),
    'achieve':       (0.540, -0.005,  0.000),
    'initial_ch':    (0.264, -0.137, -0.247),
    'internal_ch':   (0.062,  0.006, -0.025),
    'ch_vowel':      (1.064,  0.359, -0.801),
    'che_consonant': (0.992,  0.457, -0.096),
    'long_vowel':    (0.657, -0.041, -0.388),
    'repeated_ch':  (-0.500,  0.144, -0.384),
    'recent_ch':     (0.167, -0.058, -0.106),
    'che_vowel':     (0.639,  0.000,  0.000),
    'consonant':     (0.154, -0.054, -0.012),
    'check':         (0.653,  0.028,  0.000),
}


@lru_cache(maxsize=20000)
def spelling(text):
    foreign_letters = any(ord(c) > 127 and c.isalpha() for c in text)
    if foreign_letters and not HAN.search(text):
        return anyascii(text).lower(), True
    return text.lower(), foreign_letters


def pattern(s, word, previous):
    i, j, k = s.rfind('ch'), word.rfind('ch'), previous.rfind('ch')
    continues = bool(s) and s[0].isalpha()
    recent = continues and j >= 0 and len(word) - j - 2 <= 4
    if i >= 0 and (recent or s.count('ch') > 1):
        return 'repeated_ch', 1.
    if continues and k >= 0 and len(previous) - k - 2 <= 1:
        length = min(15, len(s.strip()))
        vowel = s[0] in 'aeiou'
        after_che = previous[k+2:] == 'e'
        if length <= 3:
            if vowel:
                return ('che_vowel' if after_che else 'ch_vowel'), 1.
            if after_che:
                return 'che_consonant', 1.
        return ('long_vowel' if vowel else 'consonant'), 1 / max(1, length-1)
    if i >= 0:
        if 'check' in s:
            return 'check', 1.
        if 'achiev' in s:
            return 'achieve', 1.
        if len(s[:i].lstrip()) <= 1:
            scale = 1 / sqrt(max(1, min(15, len(s)-i-2)))
            return ('che' if s[i+2:].startswith('e') else 'initial_ch'), scale
        return 'internal_ch', 1.
    return ('recent_ch' if recent else 'none'), 1.


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != document:
        carry = (document, '', '')
    _, word, previous = carry
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    s, foreign = spelling(text)
    # Also recognize c|h when the two letters straddle a token boundary.
    effective = 'c' + s if word.endswith('c') and s.startswith('h') else s
    name, scale = pattern(effective, word, previous)
    base, capitals, non_ascii = STRENGTH[name]
    value = base + capitals * any(c.isupper() for c in text)
    value += non_ascii * foreign
    tail = TAIL.search(s)
    word = ((word + s) if tail and tail.start() == 0
            else tail[0] if tail else '')[-40:]
    return (document, word, effective), float(value * scale)

It responds to the letter pair "ch" inside words. It is strongest when a word is being
spelled out in pieces and the letters so far already contain "ch" near the start of the
word, as in Nemech|ek, Tach|ih|ara, arch|es, Che|byshev or Loch|er.

For each token (a piece of a word, or a whole word):
- a piece that continues a word whose letters so far contain "ch" gets 1 / (n + 2), where
  n is the number of letters before this piece; doubled if the word begins with a capital
  letter (a name). The earlier the "ch", the stronger the response.
- "check" and its forms (check, Check, checking, checked) get CHECK.
- any other word-initial piece containing "ch" (" chip", " Che", " chat") gets CH_START.
- the first token of each document gets DOC_START, slightly negative.
- everything else is 0.

Words are runs of letters. The current word and whether it starts with a capital are
carried from token to token, and reset at each document start.
"""

READS = ()

CHECK = 0.75       # check, Check, checking, checked, checks
CH_START = 0.1     # word-initial piece containing "ch"
DOC_START = -0.19  # first token of a document

    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    word, capital = ("", False) if new_doc else carry
    continues = word != "" and not text[:1].isspace()
    if new_doc:
        value = DOC_START
    elif text.strip().lower().startswith("chec"):
        value = CHECK
    elif continues and "ch" in (word + text).lower():
        value = (2.0 if capital else 1.0) / (len(word) + 2)
    elif "ch" in text.lower():
        value = CH_START
    else:
        value = 0.0
    for c in text:  # extend the current word; punctuation and spaces end it

What it does: it is silent inside a document and writes a strongly negative value
on the FIRST token of each document. In a packed row, a new document starts wherever
the document id changes (and at the row's first token), and the model restarts its
positions there. A first token sees only itself in attention, so its activation depends
only on which token it is. Typical values:
  - ordinary words (letters only)           about -9.5
  - mixed fragments (subwords, code bits)   about -10.4
  - punctuation                             about -5.9
  - digits and whitespace                   about -4.6
Everywhere else the component is ~0 and the program predicts 0.

This program predicts those group means. The per-token values vary a lot within each
group (the spread is about 4 nats), so this is a coarse explanation: it captures the
size and sign of the document-start spike, not the exact value for each token.

def kind(token: str) -> str:
    """Coarse class of a token's text."""
    body = token.strip()
    if body == "":
        return "space"
    if body.isalpha():
        return "word"
    if body.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if all(not c.isalnum() for c in body):
        return "punct"
    return "mixed"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if not starts_document:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, START_VALUE[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

          for p in readings.split(',')}

    '王李张刘陈杨黄赵吴周徐孙马朱胡郭何高林郑梁谢宋唐许韩冯邓曹彭'

    '石廖贾夏韦付方白邹孟熊秦邱江尹薛闫段雷侯龙史陶黎贺顾毛郝'

                   for c in unicodedata.normalize('NFD', word))

    ({'old'}, 3.0, 0.0),

    ({'current', 'common', 'local', 'correct', 'long', 'numerous'}, 0.8, -0.1),
    ({'very'}, -1.3, 0.05),
)

    letters = regex.sub(r'\p{M}', '', token.strip())

        if regex.fullmatch(r'\p{M}+', token):

FLAGS = frozenset("-+ #.0123456789")

CONVERSION_VALUE = 15.0   # %d, %s, %x, %f ...: typically 9 to 21
OTHER_LETTER_VALUE = 5.0  # strftime %Y %m %H, URL %E: typically 3 to 8


def _opens_directive(token: str) -> bool:
    """Does this token contain a `%` followed only by flags and digits, e.g. "%0", "=%."?"""
    if "%" not in token:
        return False
    return all(c in FLAGS for c in token.rsplit("%", 1)[1])


def _open_percent(token_strings, document_ids, t) -> bool:
    """Is there a `%` a few tokens back, in this document, with only flags between it and t?"""
    for back in range(1, 4):
        q = t - back
        if q < 0 or document_ids[q] != document_ids[t]:
            return False
        s = token_strings[q]
        if _opens_directive(s):
            return True
        if not all(c in FLAGS for c in s):
            return False
    return False


def _conversion(letters: str) -> bool:
    """A conversion letter, with an optional length modifier: "d", "s", "lu", "ld"."""
    for mod in LENGTH:
        if letters.startswith(mod) and len(letters) > len(mod):
            letters = letters[len(mod):]
            break
    return len(letters) == 1 and letters in CONVERSIONS


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks, docs, t = prefix.token_strings, prefix.document_ids, prefix.position
    cur = toks[t]
    # Some tokens carry their own %, such as "%x" or "%d": the letter is then the whole directive.
    if cur.startswith("%") and _conversion(cur[1:]):
        return carry, CONVERSION_VALUE
    if not _open_percent(toks, docs, t):
        return carry, 0.0
    if _conversion(cur):
        return carry, CONVERSION_VALUE
    if len(cur) == 1 and cur.isalpha():
        return carry, OTHER_LETTER_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Spelling detector for the 'mis-' / 'm + s' letter pattern inside words.

The component is bipolar and sparse. It is strongly negative on short word
fragments that spell 'mis', 'miss', 'mess', 'mes', 'mise', 'mish', 'misc', 'ises',
'esis', 'iscal' (e.g. 'mis' in 'mis-trust', 'miss' in 'Miss', 'iscal' in
'miscalculation'). Inside a word it is also negative when a piece follows an 'm'
and starts with an s-like letter (ss, ß, ſ, ş, sh, sp, so, se, sc), or with 'is'
or 'if'; a piece like 'miß' or 'miſ' is more negative still. It is positive for
'mk' and 'mill' fragments, and for pieces that follow an 'm' and start with
i+k/j/l/o/a/e or k (e.g. 'RM|K', 'M|ILL', 'M|ik'). Everything else is 0.

Predictions use only the current token and the letters of the word before it.
"""
import re

READS = ()

MIS_PIECE = re.compile(r"mis|miss|mess|mes|mise|mish|misc|mesa|mss|ises|esis|iscal")
MILL_PIECE = re.compile(r"mk|mill|mink")
S_START = re.compile(r"ss|[sß]h|[sß]p|so|sc|se|[ßſş]|ış")
IS_START = re.compile(r"i[sf]")
I_POS_START = re.compile(r"i[jkolae]|k")


def _trailing_letters(text):
    m = re.search(r"[^\W\d_]*$", text)
    return m.group(0).lower() if m else ""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    piece = cur.strip().lower()
    inside_word = (
        prefix.position > 0
        and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
        and not cur.startswith(" ")
    )
    if MIS_PIECE.fullmatch(piece):
        return None, -2.0
    if MILL_PIECE.fullmatch(piece):
        return None, 2.0
    if inside_word:
        before = _trailing_letters(prefix.text_prefixes[-2])
        low = cur.lower()
        if before.endswith("mi") and re.match(r"[ßſ]", low):
            return None, -4.0
        if before.endswith("m"):
            if S_START.match(low):
                return None, -3.0
            if IS_START.match(low):
                return None, -1.5
            if I_POS_START.match(low):
                return None, 1.0
    return None, 0.0

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:2489 — a "source code / URL" detector with mixed sign.

What it responds to (activation, in the model's own units):
  * Java/C# `import` lines: strongly NEGATIVE (about -1.9) on the `import` token that
    starts a line right after a line ending in `;`, i.e. the second and later imports of
    a Java file. A Python `import` (no `;`) is ~0.
  * `using` directives (C#): mildly negative.
  * URL scheme separators `://` and `:/` (as in `https://`): POSITIVE (about +1.4).
  * Class-member modifiers at the start of a line inside code: `public` and `protected`
    (about +1.2), `private` (+0.6), `@Override` (+0.5). Mid-line uses in prose are ~0.
  * Path slashes in strings and shell commands (` /`, ` "/`, `"/`): mildly positive (+0.5).
  * Everything else: 0. The bulk of the variance (most tokens, |activation| < 0.2) is
    diffuse and not captured by any simple concept.

Each rule is a few tokens and a line-position test, looked up in the prefix. No state is
carried between positions. Values are least-squares fits on random training text.
"""

READS = ()

IMPORT_WORDS = {"import"}
USING_WORDS = {"using"}
URL_SEPARATORS = {"://", ":/"}
PATH_SLASHES = {" /", ' "/', '"/'}
LINE_START_WEIGHTS = {"public": 1.2, "protected": 1.2, "private": 0.6, "@Override": 0.5}

IMPORT_AFTER_SEMICOLON = -1.9   # Java: `import x.y;` following a line that ends in `;`
USING_LINE = -0.6               # C#: `using ...;` at the start of a line
URL_SEPARATOR = 1.4             # `://` in a URL
PATH_SLASH = 0.5                # `/` opening a path in a string or command


def _line_start(recent: str) -> bool:
    """True if the text since the last newline (within the recent tokens) is only spaces."""
    if "\n" not in recent:
        return False
    return recent.rsplit("\n", 1)[1].strip() == ""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    # The text before this token, from the last few tokens only.
    recent = "".join(prefix.token_strings[-9:-1])
    before = recent.rstrip(" \t\r\n")

    value = 0.0
    if token in IMPORT_WORDS and before.endswith(";"):
        value = IMPORT_AFTER_SEMICOLON
    elif token in USING_WORDS and _line_start(recent):
        value = USING_LINE
    elif token in URL_SEPARATORS:
        value = URL_SEPARATOR
    elif token.strip() in LINE_START_WEIGHTS and _line_start(recent):
        value = LINE_START_WEIGHTS[token.strip()]
    elif token in PATH_SLASHES:
        value = PATH_SLASH
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 1, MLP down_proj, component 2490: a lexical detector for word fragments
that spell a "hit / chit / whit" sound after an h-, ch-, wh- or Cyrillic ч/ш onset.

What it does, in plain terms:
  * Within a word, as the word is typed piece by piece, the component switches on when
    the word so far ends in one of the fragments below. The largest values are for
    "whit", "whist", "chitt", "чист" (as in "чистый") and "чит" (as in "читать").
  * It goes negative on Latin/Greek name endings spelled "-chus", "-rchus", "-phus"
    (hipparchus, Ophiuchus, platyrhynchus).
  * Everywhere else it is near zero. The first token of a document is handled by no rule.

The word-so-far is carried from token to token: a token that starts with a space, is
punctuation, or begins a new document starts a new word.
"""

READS = ()

# word-so-far suffix -> typical activation (fitted on training rows, rounded)
TABLE = {
    "whist": 10.0,
    "whit": 5.8,
    "chitt": 5.6,
    "chicht": 4.8,
    "chit": 3.3,
    "hitt": 2.7,
    "чист": 4.5,
    "очист": 3.1,
    "чит": 1.5,
    "ничт": 5.0,
    "шах": 2.9,
    "чех": 5.4,
    "чуж": 4.9,
    "чуд": 3.3,
    "шт": 1.7,
    "чт": 1.1,
    "schutz": 3.3,
    "chus": -2.8,
    "rchus": -3.6,
    "phus": -2.0,
}
KEYS = sorted(TABLE, key=len, reverse=True)  # longest suffix wins


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word, doc = carry if carry is not None else ("", None)
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc_id = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    starts_word = (
        prefix.position == 0
        or doc_id != doc
        or token.startswith(" ")
        or not token.strip().isalpha()
    )
    word = token.lstrip(" ").lower() if starts_word else word + token.lower()
    value = 0.0
    for key in KEYS:
        if word.endswith(key):
            value = TABLE[key]
            break
    return (word, doc_id), value

"""Layer 1 MLP down_proj, component 2491: a "start of a clause or code comment" detector.

What it does: it is mostly silent, but it lights up on a few kinds of token that open
a new piece of content:
  - "that" after a verb of finding, showing, saying or believing ("found that",
    "announced that"), the clause-opening complementizer. Other "that" gets a weak value.
  - "import" (the keyword starting a Python import line).
  - comment openers "//" and "#", and "--" (also a command-line flag marker).
  - a "-" flag right after a shell command name ("grep -", "tail -", "npm test -").
  - complementizers in other languages: dass/daß, que, che, что, hogy, wenn.
It is negative on the first token of each document (after <|endoftext|>), where the
component sits at a document reset.

Values are rough means of the activation in each class, not fitted per token.
The rules are a readable approximation. Other contexts (a long tail of small values,
digits in version strings, comma after "according to ... census") are predicted as 0.
"""

READS = ()

# Verbs after which "that" opens a reported clause.
REPORT_VERBS = {
    "found", "show", "shows", "showed", "shown", "conclude", "concluded", "said", "say",
    "says", "saying", "revealed", "reveal", "indicate", "indicated", "suggest", "suggests",
    "suggested", "announced", "noted", "note", "notes", "stated", "states", "believe",
    "think", "know", "knew", "assume", "see", "mentions", "argued", "added", "claimed",
    "explained", "reports", "reported", "learned", "hope", "hoping", "feel", "felt",
}
# Command names whose following "-" starts a flag.
SHELL_COMMANDS = {
    "grep", "tail", "head", "cat", "python", "sed", "test", "run", "npm", "go", "cargo",
    "pytest", "mvn", "git", "docker", "curl", "pip", "node", "awk", "find", "ls", "make",
}
COMMENT_OPENERS = {"//", " //", "#", " #", "--", " --"}
COMPLEMENTIZERS = {" dass", " daß", " que", " che", " что", " hogy", " wenn"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if len(prefix) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, -0.3  # first token of a document
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip()
    if tok in (" that", "that"):
        return carry, 0.6 if prev in REPORT_VERBS else 0.1
    if tok == " import":
        return carry, 1.0
    if tok in COMMENT_OPENERS:
        return carry, 0.6
    if tok in (" -", "-") and prev in SHELL_COMMANDS:
        return carry, 1.0
    if tok in COMPLEMENTIZERS:
        return carry, 0.4
    return carry, 0.0
